t: How To Turn Around Difficult Students (Part 1)
q: The reason teachers struggle with difficult students year after year is because they don’t have the stomach for it. Their sense of compassion overrides doing what is right for the student.
But this same compassion that in many respects makes you a good teacher can cause you to make excuses for students, which, in the long run, hurt them and undermine your ability to turn them around.
Are you ready to say, “It’s over. The buck stops here. The disrespect, the bad behavior, and the excuses are going to stop with me?

You really can make a difference in Anthony’s life. You really can change the course of his life and lead him down the path that leads to success and opportunity—despite the terrible hand Anthony has been dealt.
And by excusing bad behavior and blaming it on outside influences, you’re letting them know loud and clear that you don’t believe in them.

t: How To Make Classroom Management Sticky https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/02/20/how-to-make-classroom-management-sticky/
q: She then explained that the brown-eyed students were smarter and superior to the blue-eyed students and therefore would be allowed extra recess.
While in the inferior group, students described feeling “sad,” “bad,” “stupid,” and “mean.” They were so affected by the negative label that even their academic performance dropped.
What Jane Elliot did was remarkable. She took something abstract to her students—discrimination—and turned it into a concrete experience.
When it comes to classroom management, scratch-the-surface teaching isn’t going to cut it. To make your rules, expectations, and procedures sticky, they must be made into an experience.
To get your students to meet your expectations and behave as you desire, you must show them exactly what you want.
Make them prove to you they understand your rules and procedures by actually performing them.
Classroom management is more effective when students are able to experience what you want from them—rather than merely being told what you want.

t: How To Get Students To Raise Their Hand https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/02/13/how-to-get-your-students-to-raise-their-hand/
q: Calling out is a momentum killer of the highest order and can turn a well-planned lesson into a halting mess.
Every student has a right to participate, not just those who are more assertive. If calling out is allowed, a segment of your classroom will rarely be heard from.
Students who participate do better than those who don’t. Allowing students to call out gives socially confident students an unfair advantage.
Your students need to know exactly what you expect from them. The most effective way to do this is to sit in a student’s chair, and show them precisely how you want them to raise their hand.
Show your students how not to raise their hand. Act out common unacceptable behaviors.
If a student calls out and waves their hand at you, first ignore them. Send the message that you don’t respond to anything except proper hand raising.
I’ve never known a teacher who was lax in this area and didn’t have problems with student behavior, learning, engagement, time management, and more.

t: Why Having Fun Makes Classroom Management Easier ment-easier/
q: There is no getting around the fact that students who are happy to be in school, learn and behave better than those who don’t. It makes perfect sense, yet many teachers miss this simple truth.

It occurred to me in that moment that John was teaching without a net (i.e., no classroom management plan). Although he was quick to correct students who interfered with learning, he didn’t seem to have any specified rules or consequences.
John wasted a lot of time and energy reminding students of this and that and asking for quiet so he could speak—which could have been avoided if he had had a classroom management plan.

John was so much fun, and his lessons so interesting, that his students would have done anything to be a part of his class, including behaving in whatever manner he deemed acceptable—however unspecified that was.
Adding some fun to your classroom isn’t difficult. It doesn’t take a lot of pre-planning and you don’t need any special talent. It just takes a willingness to make it a priority.
Your students will appreciate it, and you’ll add more leverage to your classroom management plan.
